title: In the evening, love (Sayings of Light and Love)
hookLine: at the end we will be judged on love

lines: THE FINAL EXAM OF YOUR LIFE.
cards: A final exam with a whole life on it. What would the questions be? The easy guess is a report card.
How much got done. How much got earned. Were the rules kept.
How many people know the name. Maybe a section on religion: enough prayers, enough Sundays, the right beliefs. John of the Cross wrote down what he thought would be on that exam.
It's one line, from a small collection of his sayings, short enough to fit on your palm. Today's word is how it begins.

teach.b: First, the sayings. Tradition says John wrote short, sharp sayings on slips of paper for the friars and nuns he guided. They were gathered later as the Sayings of Light and Love.
Some are a single sentence. Second, the line. In John's Spanish: "A la tarde te examinarán en el amor."
In the evening, you will be examined in love. The evening is the end of life. The exam has one subject.
Not how much you knew about prayer, or how many dark nights you understood. Love. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes this line when it teaches about judgment.
Third, where he got it. It's not John's invention.
It comes straight from Jesus's picture of the last judgment in Matthew's Gospel, where the nations are sorted by whether they fed the hungry, welcomed the stranger, visited the sick and the prisoner.
The king says, in the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."
John knew this passage from both sides: the boy washing the sick in the hospital, the prisoner in the dark room. Fourth, what to do about it.
Near the end of his life, John wrote to a Carmelite nun who was upset at how his superiors were treating him.
He told her not to grieve over it, and added: where there is no love, put love, and you will draw out love.

teach.h: WHERE THERE IS NO LOVE, PUT LOVE.
A LA TARDE TE EXAMINARÁN EN EL AMOR.
teach.b: The nights, the fire, the nada all come back to this. The whole point was love.

how: Catholics often quote John's saying on the evening of life, which the Catechism cites in its teaching on judgment, and many make an evening examen asking how they loved that day.

games.q: a nun writes to John, upset at how his own superiors are treating him. what does he tell her?
o: where there is no love, put love, and you will draw out love.
games.why: that's his line in a letter from the last year of his life: don't grieve over it, put love there.

practice: Picture this evening, the end of today, and look back on it: what would love have done?
Let one face come to mind, someone hungry, lonely, sick, difficult, or simply waiting to hear from you, and ask what one thing love needs you to do for them.
If you pray, ask God to show you; if you don't, trust the first honest answer.
